objetivo.en: Greet people, say goodbye, thank them and apologize in Spanish, using pure vowels and the right r sound.

nota.en: Used both to greet and to say goodbye after dark.

With an accent mark. Without it, «si» means «if».
Single r between vowels: one quick tap, like the «tt» in American «butter».
Double rr: a strong trill (a rolled r).

explicacion.en: «tardes» is a feminine word, so it takes «buenas». Only «días» takes «buenos»: buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches.
«días» is masculine even though it ends in -as: buenos días.

texto.en: Every unit follows the same path: first we teach you with examples, then you practice with hints, and finally you check what you know. Tap the speaker to hear every word. Good news: Spanish spelling is almost phonetic, so once you know a few rules you can read nearly anything aloud.

Spanish has only five vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u. Keep them short and pure; never let them glide as in English «no» (noh-oo) or «day» (dey-ee). The h is always silent: hola = «OH-lah». ñ sounds like «ny»: mañana. A single r between vowels is a quick tap (pero), while rr is a trill (perro). A written accent (´) marks the stressed syllable: adiós, perdón, días.

titulo.en: Yo, tú, usted: pronouns and politeness

objetivo.en: Name people with subject pronouns, choose between tú and usted, and understand why Spanish often drops the subject.

nota.en: With an accent: tú = you. Without it, tu = your.
With an accent: él = he. Without it, el = the.
ll sounds like the «y» in «yes» in most of Latin America.
In Spain, friends say «vosotros». You'll hear it, but in Latin America everyone uses «ustedes».

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Buenos días, señor García. ¿Cómo está usted?

explicacion.en: With señor or señora + last name, use the formal usted: «¿Cómo está usted?».
A group of only women is «ellas». «Ellos» is for men or mixed groups.

texto.en: The subject pronouns are: yo (I), tú (you), usted (you, formal), él (he), ella (she), nosotros/nosotras (we), ustedes (you all), ellos/ellas (they). Spanish marks gender in the plural: nosotras and ellas are for groups of women only; a mixed group uses nosotros and ellos.

English has one «you»; Spanish has two for one person. Use tú with friends, family, children and people your age in relaxed settings. Use usted with older people, strangers in formal settings, officials and anyone you call señor or señora. For more than one person, Latin America always uses ustedes. When in doubt, start with usted.

In Spanish the verb ending already shows who is doing something, so the pronoun is usually dropped: «¿Cómo estás?» already means «how are you?» with tú. You add the pronoun for contrast or emphasis, as in «¿Y tú?» (and you?). Usted is often kept to sound clear and polite: «¿Cómo está usted?».

titulo.en: Ser: who you are and where you're from

objetivo.en: Say who someone is, what they do and where they are from with ser (soy, eres, es, somos, son).

nota.en: Same form for men and women.
No accent: mi = my; mí (with accent) = me.
The x is pronounced like a Spanish j: «MEH-hee-ko».

explicacion.en: Unlike English «I am a student», Spanish drops the article with professions: «Soy estudiante», «Es médica».
Each person has its own form: yo → soy. And you can drop «yo»: «Soy de Inglaterra».

titulo.en: Ser: one of two «to be» verbs

texto.en: Spanish has two verbs for «to be». Ser is for identity: who someone is, their job, their nationality or origin. Its present forms: yo soy, tú eres, él/ella/usted es, nosotros somos, ellos/ellas/ustedes son. Remember to drop the pronoun: «Soy Ana» sounds more natural than «Yo soy Ana». With jobs there's no «a»: «Soy estudiante». Many nouns change for gender: profesor → profesora, médico → médica.
To say where someone is from, use ser + de + place: «Soy de México» (I'm from Mexico). It's always ser, never estar, because your origin is part of your identity.

ejemplos.texto: Mateo es de México. Es mi amigo.

titulo.en: Estar: how and where you are

objetivo.en: Say how you feel and where you are with estar, and choose between ser and estar.

nota.en: The accent matters: está (is) vs. esta (this).

explicacion.en: How you feel is a state, so use estar: «Estoy cansado».
Where a person is uses estar: «Está en casa».
The adjective agrees with the person: a woman is «cansada», a man is «cansado».

texto.en: Ser tells you what or who something is. Estar tells you how or where it is: feelings, temporary states and location. A rhyme to remember: «How you feel and where you are, that's when you use estar». Present forms: yo estoy, tú estás, él/ella/usted está, nosotros estamos, ellos/ellas/ustedes están. Compare: «Soy Ana» (identity) and «Estoy cansada» (state).
Spanish adjectives match the person they describe. Most end in -o for a man and -a for a woman: Mateo está cansado, Lucía está cansada. Bien and mal never change.

Make sentences negative with no, and ask and answer simple questions with ¿…?, dónde, quién and cómo.

explicacion.en: «No» goes right before the verb, not after it.
After a question word, the verb usually comes before the subject: ¿Dónde está Ana?
Question words carry a written accent: ¿dónde?, ¿quién?, ¿cómo?

texto.en: To make a sentence negative, just put «no» right before the verb. There's no helper like «do» or «don't»: «No soy de México» (I'm not from Mexico), «No estoy cansado» (I'm not tired). When you answer a question, you often hear «no» twice: the first means «no», the second means «not»: «No, no soy médico».

traduccion.en: I'm not tired. (said by a woman)

texto.en: Spanish opens every question with ¿ and every exclamation with ¡, so you know from the start how to read it: ¿Eres de México? ¡Hola! A yes/no question can keep the same word order as the statement; your voice rises at the end. Question words carry an accent (¿dónde?, ¿quién?, ¿cómo?) and are usually followed by the verb: ¿Dónde está Mateo? To agree, say «Yo también» (me too), or «Yo tampoco» (me neither) after a negative.

traduccion.en: Are you from Canada? Yes, of course.
I'm a student. And you? Me too.

objetivo.en: Say your name, where you're from and where you live, and ask someone else, using tú or usted.

nota.en: Literally «I call myself». ll sounds like the «y» in «yes».

traduccion.en: pleased to meet you (said by a man)
pleased to meet you (said by a woman)

explicacion.en: «Me llamo» already contains the verb. Don't add «es» as in English «my name is».
«Encantado/encantada» agrees with the speaker: a woman says «encantada», a man says «encantado». «Mucho gusto» works for everyone.

texto.en: To say your name, use «Me llamo…» (literally «I call myself…»), or simply «Soy…». To ask: «¿Cómo te llamas?» with tú, or «¿Cómo se llama usted?» with usted. Notice that Spanish asks «how» (cómo), not «what».

For origin you already know «Soy de…» and «¿De dónde eres?»; with usted, ask «¿De dónde es usted?». For where you live: «Vivo en Lima» and «¿Dónde vives?». When you meet someone, say «Mucho gusto» (anyone) or «Encantado» (if you're a man) / «Encantada» (if you're a woman). The other person may answer «Igualmente» (likewise).
